courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Anthropology of Film
courses.description: This course will introduce anthropological approaches to the study of the visual and pictorial world. Classic and recent ethnographic films will be shown, and students are guided to an anthropological understanding through pictorial media. Entertainment motion pictures and documentary films will also be analysed as an anthropological issue, especially in relation to such notions as "culture", "otherness" and "reality".
courses.learning_outcomes:
1. Students will learn about major visual anthropological theories and various styles of films around the world as well as relevant current discussion on objectivity, reality and self-reflexivity.

2. Students will be guided in examining changing cultural values in different countries and become more conscious of aspects of culture that they take for granted through the investigation of ethnographic film.

3. Students will learn about different local lifestyles and their interaction with the changing living environment, and to develop an understanding of the role of tradition and globalization.

4. After the course, students will appreciate the diversity of culture and the processes that mold and shape cultural identity.

5. Students will also learn skills in research design, cultural data collection, ethnographic film-making, and presentation of results.
courses.course_syllabus:
Do you want to know more about different developments of

ethnographic films, documentary films, propaganda films, and

entertainment films? Do you want to know the history of films in

different countries with different styles and topics? This course

provides a visual anthropological approach to the study of cultures and

social development through films. Teaching materials will include

ethnographies, popular writings, documentary films, ethnographic films,

movies etc. in order to provide students with a comprehensive approach

for understanding the diversity of film and cultural representation in

various countries.

Class Performance: 20%

Two Short Film Reports: 40%

Essay: 40%

Most updated assessment will be announced in class.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Gender and Culture
courses.description:
(UGEC2653 is double-coded with ANTH2310.)

This course looks at the relationship between gender and culture, by comparing women and men in societies with different modes of production and social organization. Through analysing gender roles, enculturation process, kinship, division of labour by gender, power and control and social development, students will understand how culture influences the concept of gender and its related behaviour among human groups.
courses.enrollment_requirement: Not for students who have taken GENA2192 or UGEC2653
courses.learning_outcomes:
After taking this course, students will be able to:

* analyze gender and sexual diversities in different cultures
* explain how gender and culture can be studied systematically
* discuss major theories explaining gender and sexuality and use those theories to explain contemporary gender issues
* demonstrate how taken-for-granted ideas of gender shape our everyday lives

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Culture and Mind
courses.description: How can we understand the minds of other people? Do people in different cultures or societies feel and think in different ways? How do childhood experiences affect people and shape or even determine what kinds of persons they will become? What is it like to be mentally abnormal or even pathological? Do people in different cultures or societies experience, understand, and treat psychopathology in different ways? This course examines psychological experiences—feelings, perceptions, thoughts, and motivations—from social and cross-cultural perspectives. It sets out to explore the intersection between anthropology, a field that typically turns to the exotic other, and psychology, a field that often takes the universality of mental activities and mechanisms for granted. Specific focus is placed upon how ethnographers, clinicians, and researchers with training in both fields grapple with various mental phenomena and different ways of understanding them. As most of the materials are drawn from psychological anthropology, this course also serves as an eclectic introduction to this subfield, which was once influential in the history of American anthropology.
courses.learning_outcomes:
1. Students will acquire solid knowledge of cross-cultural comparisons of psychological experiences and their understandings.

2. Students will gain comprehension of the key debates about the universality and relativity of human emotions and individual behavior.

3. Students will think more critically, and develop practical skills and knowledge, about how to understand the minds of other people who are either from the same culture or society or not.

4. Students will achieve comprehension of the major ideas in psychological anthropology, the development in this field and the relationship of psychological anthropology to the general discipline of cultural anthropology.
courses.course_syllabus:
This course introduces students to the studies of psychological experiences from social and cross-cultural perspectives. It examines the intersection between anthropology and psychology, with a specific focus on how ethnographers, clinicians, and researchers with training in both fields grapple with various mental phenomena and different ways of understanding them.

Week 1. Introduction

The course is divided into three parts. The first part “Depth Psychology and Its Cultural Formulations” begins with the Freudian psychoanalysis and its discovery of the unconscious, which has almost become the hallmark of the modern mind. This is followed by a discussion on the encounter of psychoanalysis with 19th-century anthropology that has resulted in imaginative meditations on culture and civilization.

Week 2. The Discovery of the Unconscious

Week 3. Is Oedipus Complex Universal?

Week 4. Culture as Collective Neurosis

Week 5. Civilization and Its Effects

The second part “Culture and Personality and Beyond” deals with some of the most serious endeavors to explore the minds of non-western cultures and societies from the side of anthropology, with a particular focus on the “culture and personality” school that once dominated American anthropology in the middle of the 20th century. The most important strands of studies that derived from it, including comparative childhood studies, phenomenology, and ethnopsychology, are also introduced here.

Week 6. From Configurations to National Characters

Week 7. Cultural and Personality with a Psychoanalytic Bent

Week 8. Comparative Childhood Studies

Week 9. Phenomenology and Ethno-psychology

The last part of the course “The Abnormal Mind” shifts the focus to psychopathology. It begins with culture-bound syndromes that once flourished in the literature of transcultural psychiatry, followed by an extended discussion on the psychotic condition—a fundamental human mental process—and its institutional treatment, and ends with the latest efforts in anthropology to explore the individual mind in society.

Week 10. Culture-Bound Syndromes

Week 11. The Psychotic Mind

Week 12. The Asylum

Week 13. Explorations of Subjectivity

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: From Madness to Mental Health
courses.description: This course examines mental illness and mental health as subjective experiences, social processes, and objects of scientific knowledge and practice. It invites students to explore human experiences that are labelled as abnormal or pathological, to understand the expert knowledge and technologies employed to remedy these conditions, and to think about the complex relationships between them and the broader social and cultural contexts. Readings are drawn from psychiatric anthropology or anthropology of mental health, clinical case studies, and memoirs. They are chosen to reflect an interdisciplinary scope that includes social sciences, psychiatry itself, and the layman’s/patient’s perspective.
courses.learning_outcomes:
Our goal is that after taking this course, you will have:

1. To analyze psychiatry as a cultural domain and a social institution as well as a critical concern for mental health as a social issue.

2. To understand the symptomatology and illness experiences of major mental illnesses.

3. To evaluate how mental illness and mental health interact with local social and cultural contexts in different cultural context.

4. To apply anthropological knowledge and skills in personal as well as social mental health matters.
courses.course_syllabus:
* *Module 1: Origins and Framings**

* *The first part of the course examines three of the most important origins of modern mental health that continue to shape our current knowledge and practice:** **(1) Asylum psychiatry that offers custodial care of people with severe mental illness.** **(2) Psychoanalysis that pioneers the talk therapy for common mental disorders.** **(3) Colonial psychiatry that puts in place the international dissemination of psychiatric knowledge and practice.**

Insanity and the Birth of Asylum

Hysteria and the Birth of Psychoanalysis

From Colonial Psychiatry to Global Mental Health

* *Module 2: Mental Illness in Context**

* *The second part of the course makes foray into a series of ethnographic examples. Each week we examine a major category of mental illness or psychopathology****—****including psychosis, depression, dissociation, addiction, and so on****—****through case studies, in which culturally-mediated experiences and social courses of illnesses will be revealed.**

Psychotic/Extraordinary Experience

Depression

Trauma and PTSD

Addiction

Eating Disorders

Psychopathy and Criminality

* *Module 3: Mental Health in Contemporary Society**

* *The third part of the course discusses some of the most pressing mental health trends we are witnessing in contemporary times, including the rise of big pharmaceutical companies,** **the dominance of neuroscience, and the popularity of self-help and self-healing measures. In the end we will try to envision a better future for psychiatry and mental health services.**

Pharma and Neuro

Self-Help and Recovery

The Future of Psychiatry

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Environmental Crises and Cultures of Survival
courses.description:
(UGEC2950 is double-coded with ANTH2380.)

This course pays attention to the environment and its relation with human experiences. Through the lens of environment, we bring human diversity into presence, examining ways of life of peoples—from Indonesia highlander to Tokyo urbanites—and their words and deeds to tackle crises of planetary scale—climate change, nuclear disaster, air pollution, waste, deforestation. Facing these crises, can anthropological inquiry of the environment help us to explore a humanity that can accommodate living beings of all kind? How can such inquiry inspire us to make changes that create a world we can live together?

We’ll follow these trails in the environment to look for engagement and conversation: cultural perception on the origin of agriculture, resource use and religious belief, debating traditional ecological knowledge, globalization and state intervention, environmental justice, land dispossession, waste and pollution, disaster and extreme environment. Through ethnographies of people who are struggling to survive, this course asks why they are pushed into poverty, how their resources being exploited, what they do to fight for justice; it covers SDGs related to the issues of sustainable agriculture (SDG2), tacking climate change (SDG13) and promoting peace, justice and institutional accountability (SDG16).
courses.course_attributes:
SDG-GE #2 Zero Hunger
SDG-GE #13 Climate Action
SDG-GE #16 Peace, Justice and Strong Institutions
courses.course_syllabus:
* *Part I: Cultural Knowledge of the Environment**

1. Cultural Perceptions of the Origin of Agriculture

2. Religious Belief in Resource Use

3. Traditional Ecological Knowledge

4. Materialist Conception of Nature (I)

5. Materialist Conception of Nature (II)—State Intervention and Globalization

* *Part II: Contemporary Culture of Environmental Politics**

Topics of contemporary environmental crises are contemplated through case studies and ethnographies of people who become vulnerable. We will cover related SDGs to explore possibilities of action to achieve a sustainable way of life for humans.

6. Extraction (SDG16)

- the cause of uneven distribution of environmental risks and how local communities struggle for survival and justice

7. Waste

8. Toxicity

9. Disaster and extreme environment (SDG16)

- the government’s immediate response to disaster and affected communities’ action to restore respectful life

10. Conservation (SDG2)

- the functioning of conservation agencies and the conflicts between conservation and local community

11. Climate Change (SDG 13)

- the impact of climate change to local ecology and people’s livelihood, their actions and adaptations

12. Conclusion—Rethinking Development (SDG 16)

- the insistence on productivity in modern societies, and the possibilities of sustainable future

1) understand the world's cultural diversity and human universals.

2) know anthropology's subfields, and be able to think using their ideas.

3) comprehend and be able to apply the different theories explaining sociocultural phenomena

4) be able, using anthropological modes of understanding, to think critically and perceptively about one's society and the world.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Understanding Islam
courses.description: This class begins its study of Islam by examining the historical developments of Islam in pre-Islamic Arabia and looking at the life of various religious figures. It then examines aspects of Islamic civilization, culture and philosophy. Finally it addresses issues of the so-called ‘politicization of religion’ in the context of globalizing modernity and violent conflict. Throughout this course we will investigate the insights that anthropological analyses can offer to discussions centering the relations between Muslim societies and the West.
courses.learning_outcomes:
• Study and appreciate the contemporary cultural diversity, values and world views of Muslims living in diverse circumstances and spaces

• Introduce the contemporary struggles over religious authority and orthodoxy in some parts of the Muslim world

• To identify with the ideas and practices relating to gender, education and art

• To assist students in understanding and appreciating the complexity of the lives of Muslims in the contemporary world

• Challenge and think critically about existing stereotypes about Muslims and Islam

• Think critically and constructively about the issues that are discussed

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Political Violence and Human Rights
courses.description:
(UGED2622 is double-coded with ANTH2530.)

This course examines the pervasiveness of violence from an anthropological and comparative perspective. We consider a wide range of phenomena that can be called violence within diverse historical and cultural contexts. Violence is always political – whether it is manifest in the spectacular practices of torture, terrorism, or genocide, or the invisible structures of inequalities that generate educational, health, and food inequities. Specifically, we will address four SDG goals in depth: SDG#1 No Poverty, SDG #5 “Gender Equality”, SDG# 8 Decent Work and Economic Growth, SDG #10 “Reduced Inequalities” and SDG #16 “Peace, Justice and strong institutions”; The topics covered will be understood in relation to histories of colonialism and nationalism, ideologies about race, gender, and variant forms of social, economic, and political hierarchies. We further examine the effectiveness and limitations of human rights and humanitarianism as remedies, including the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).

courses.course_syllabus:
The course is divided into four parts:

* *Part I offers a conceptual introduction that will provide students with the tools to analyze issues of violence and human rights in the world today. (Overall view of the United Nations, and the SDGs)**

Topic 1. Can violence be apolitical? Can human rights be wrong?

Topic 2. The politics of representation – Violence and Rights

Topic 3. Violence as a spectrum and knowledge production
Topic 4 Human rights as cultural practice

* *Part II considers through empirical studies the agents and structures of violence (SGD 1, 8, 10, 16)**

Topic 5. The Banality of Evil: Police as Agents of State Violence

Topic 6. What does State Violence Look Like?

Topic 7. National Borders and National Security: Violence and Order

* *Part III considers the gender and sexuality as matrixes of inequalities (SDG 1, 5, 8, 16)**

Topic 8. Sexual Violence in Conflicts

Topic 9. Sex Trafficking and the problem of Neoliberalism

* *Part IV considers global migration and humanitarianism (SDG 1, 8, 16)**

Topic 10. The Violence of Exclusion: Forced Migration and Refugees

Topic 11. The Violence of Humanitarinaism

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Race, Mobility, and Belonging
courses.description: This course is designed to stimulate reflections on race, racialization, identity, and migration through a series of ethnographic studies and big picture questions. What is race? What is racialization? How does racialization occur and how is it experienced, especially by people on the move? How does the way we look shape our identity and a sense of inclusion or exclusion from society? How does it influence our life choices and trajectories? By following Clarence Gravlee, we will analyze how race becomes biology, i.e., how “race” as a socially constructed category becomes an embodied experience with profound impact on our health and everyday life. We will learn to analyze the racialization discourses, which sometimes rely on the alternative words such as “culture” or “ethnicity” in the essentializing, biologizing manner. We will then see how such discourses are implicated in migration policy, media, education, science, medical practice, and capitalism. While accounting for global issues, the course aims to center Asia as a site for examining the interconnected histories of empire, mobility, and belonging. Comparative examples from other parts of the world will situate Asia in global discussions of racialized mobility. We will engage with key theories and ethnographies addressing “race” in the intersection with other aspects of social differences—gender, class, religion, and language— and examine how such intersections shape experiences of migration and belonging.
courses.learning_outcomes:
By the end of this course, students will be able to do the following:

* Name and explain major anthropological theories of race and racialization
* Understand race as a product of political and social processes rather than a biological fact
* Identify processes and discourses of racialization in ethnographic contexts
* Explain main concepts in the anthropology of transnational mobility and belonging, and show how the discussions of “race” have been integral to such studies
* Analyze how migration influences racialization and the practices of exclusion and inclusion
* Compare and analyze the politics, discourses, and experiences of whiteness, blackness, Chineseness, mixed race, etc. in Asia and beyond
* Critically assess the role of racialization in migration policy, citizenship, minority education, labor, life opportunities, access to information, and healthcare.
* Apply the acquired knowledge to an individual ethnographic project and one’s everyday life
courses.course_syllabus:
Week 1 – Introduction: Anthropology and the Question of Race

In this class, students will be introduced to the course, its scope, some key concepts, course objectives, assessment, grading policy, reading, and overall expectation. An introductory lecture will focus on the history of anthropological approaches to race from biological determinism to social construction and embodiment, reflecting on the question of how the discipline of anthropology has both reinforced and challenged the concept of race historically.

Week 2 – How Does Race Become Biology?

This class will focus on contemporary understandings of race in anthropology, but it will also draw from other disciplines, such as Critical Race Studies. Students will be introduced to the concept of racialization and learn how it differs from the concept of racial formation. They will also gain a deeper understanding of how racialized categorization and discrimination produce real, embodied experiences. In particular, we will use ethnographic examples from medical anthropology to analyze how racialization results in stress and poor health.

Week 3 – Racialized Governance and Mobility

In this week racialization will be analyzed in the context of human mobility, particularly colonial expansion and contemporary migration. By looking at historical cases globally and in Asia, we will examine how racial hierarchies were embedded in colonial knowledge production and governance, including the policies related to eugenics, settler colonialism, reservations, miscegenation, etc. This class will then open a door to the following weeks, by initiating a discussion of how modern states regulate human mobility by invoking racialized categories, and how such categories make affective impacts on people’s lives.

Week 4 – Gender, Race, and Intimacy

Students will be introduced to the concept of intersectionality to understand how the experiences of migrants are shaped by how they are viewed as both racialized and gendered subjects. We will reflect on sexuality, migration, and body politics. What forms of power and racialized intimacy emerge in transnational domestic and romantic labor?

Week 5 – Class, “Skill,” and Transnational Migration

Today’s topics are labor migration and neoliberal economies. We will see how race intersects with class in global migrant flows, by particularly addressing how governments produce the discourse on “skill” and the accompanied categories of “skilled” and “unskilled” work. In particular, we will reflect on the differences between “migrant” and “expatriate.” By engaging with the concept of racial capitalism, students will debate about how transnational work migration and capitalist regimes reproduce and contest class inequalities.

Week 6 – Privilege

Building on the previous week, we will continue exploring raced, classed, and other dimensions of privilege, both nationally and transnationally. We will examine theoretical approaches to privilege, by employing the concepts of invisible privilege, precarious privilege, etc. to better understand how skin color, “blood,” and caste emerge as racialized markers of superiority or subordination.

Week 7 – Whiteness in Asia and the world

This week addressing specifically the category of “whiteness” using western contexts and Asia. We will explore the theoretical debates on the universal relevance of the white privilege framework. We will also examine how various group have been racialized as “white” or others, depending on historical and geographical circumstances.

Week 8 – Skin, blood, and roots

How does racialization impact nationhood, legality, and cultural belonging? How do states define and discipline belonging through racialized citizenship regimes? How do racialized migrant groups navigate between their desire to maintain difference and claiming inclusion?

Week 9 – Race by other means

This week is about ideologies of color-blindness in societies and contexts which claim to have transcended racism and where the word “race” is absent. Yet, as scholars show, other words such as “culture” continue to be deployed in essentializing, biologizing ways. Students will learn about racialization that occurs without the term race and will be able to analyze how “culture,” “religion,” and “ethnic minority” carry racialized meanings. They will reflect on xenophobia and islamophobia, asking how religion, culture, and race shape each other in contexts of migration and belonging.

Week 10 – Racialization and Belonging in Hong Kong

This week’s lecture and discussions are focused on Hong Kong and its diverse communities, such as asylum seekers, foreign domestic workers, locally born ethnic minorities, etc. We will reflect on the production of racialized difference in media, education, and public discourse.

Week 11 – Language, Accent, and Racialization

In this week students will be introduced to the concept of indexicality to discuss how language and accent signal one’s belonging to a certain classed, raced, and migrant group. We will also explore the theories of language ideologies and linguistic hierarchies. We will discuss how the state and other institutions of power deploy language to represent, manage, and control migrants; and how migrants creatively deploy language to push back.

Week 12 – Race and Technology

This week will cover a broad range of questions related to the role of technology in perpetuating or altering racailzed politics, knowledge claims, and sentiment. In what ways does technology reproduce or transform racialization, migration, and belonging? We will examine how the development of new genomics technologies and DNA ancestry testing contribute to the shifting meanings of race, citizenship, and identity. We will also look at the emergence of digital diasporas, algorithmic bias, and virtual race.

Week 13 – Futures of Race, Migration, and Citizenship

The concluding week will provide an opportunity for the students to present on their research projects and reflect on new trajectories of the race and migration scholarship.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Religion and Culture
courses.description: Religious practices and beliefs permeate cultures throughout the world and religion has always been one of the most important topics in anthropology and liberal studies. This course examines the following aspects of religion: magic and sorcery, symbolism and ritual, gender and religion, shamanism, syncretism, and social change driven by religious ideas. The course also introduces major traditions of social theory: each tradition offers a different way of looking at the role of religion in people's lives. This course thus introduces students to various forms of religious expression around the world and also exposes them to different interpretations of religion.
courses.learning_outcomes:
1. Students will be familiar with the major anthropological theories of religion.

2. Students will learn about the major religions and some indigenous peoples’ beliefs and practices.

3. Students will learn about religious tolerance and avoid religiocentrism.

4. Students will have a greater understanding of religions and human societies.
courses.course_syllabus:
This course aims to introduce students to some anthropological approaches to the study of religions. Students will learn to appreciate the diversity of religions as well as their functions in human societies. In addition, students will learn about the major world religions, as well as Chinese and some other indigenous religious traditions. The significance of religion in present and future human societies will be discussed, too.

Course Grading

Participation: 15%

Mid-term test: 30%

Final quiz: 15%

Final project paper: 40%

Most updated assessment will be announced in class.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Indian Culture and Society
courses.description: This course is an anthropological exploration of the social life and cultures of India. We will explore India through the lens of popular culture, caste and class, the politics of religion, gender/sexuality, nationalism and globalization. Students will be engaged in the contemporary theoretical debates relating to the socio-cultural change in modern India, enabling them to appreciate the complex nature of Indian culture and Indian nationality.
courses.learning_outcomes:
• To gain an understanding of the diversity of the region

• Understand the evolution of Indian culture and civilization from pre-historic to post-Vedic era

• To get a glimpse of India’s colonial history and its postcolonial implications

• Demonstrate the unity inherent in India’s diversity and pluralism

• Help the student’s understand the processes of socio-cultural change occurring in modern India

• Develop a critical understanding amongst the students of the role Bollywood films play in the lives of the Indian population and issues arising thereof

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Diaspora: Migration, Identity and Ethnicity
courses.description: This course examines the cultural phenomena of migration of populations, immigration across national boundaries, and the displacement of peoples and communities. This course uses the diaspora cultures, such as the ethnic Chinese, the Jewish communities and the ethnic Indians, to illustrate the history, structure, theory and politics of ethnic identity, ethnic relations, and cultural and national identity.
courses.learning_outcomes:
After taking this course, students will:

1) Understand theories of ethnic identity formation

2) Comprehend global processes of migration

2) Be able to apply these theories and ideas to situations around the world today

4) Be able to use these theories and ideas to think critically and perceptively about identity and migration present and future

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Cultures of Chinese Overseas
courses.description: This course will introduce students to the study of Chinese communities outside China. Ethnic Chinese communities worldwide may be considered as comprising an ethnological field. Due to the sharing of aspects of Chinese civilization, Chinese everywhere share some cultural similarities. However, the need to adapt to different ecological, political and socio-cultural environments calls for adaptation and transformation. Thus the diverse Chinese communities worldwide are ideal for comparative studies, especially on a number of anthropological/ sociological themes such as cultural continuity and transformation, cultural identities and ethnic identities, ethnic relations, social organization, and so on.
courses.learning_outcomes:
1) To become familiar with Chinese migration and life in different parts of the world

2) To gain appreciation for cultural diversity among Chinese in different parts of the world

3) To understand the nature of transnational networks among Chinese overseas and with China

4) To be aware of not essentializing identities and to respect diverse and multiple ethnic identification

5) To gain a basic knowledge of ethnic Chinese studies
courses.course_syllabus:
In this course you will learn about Chinese communities worldwide. There is much that we can learn from the diverse experiences of migration and settlement of Chinese in different parts of the world. While this is an anthropological course, our readings will be interdisciplinary. The topics that we will discuss include:

1. Introduction: Labels and the Study of Chinese Overseas

2. Migration and Diaspora

3. Chinese Migration: Asia

4. Chinese Migration: The Americas

5. Chinese in Europe and Russia

6. Chinese in Australasia and Africa

7. Localization, Ethnogenesis and Identities

8. Cultural Reproduction and Identity

9. Family, Kinship, Transnational Networks and China

10. Global Capitalism, Transnationalism and China

11. Migration, Remigration and Homelands

Course Requirements

1. Participation (10%)

2. Mid-term exam (30%)

3. Quiz on the topics taught after mid-term test (20%)

4. Final project paper of around 10 pages, double-spaced (40%)

Updated assessment will be announced in class.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Anthropological Field Study
courses.description:
This course will enable students to extend their anthropological learning in the classroom to an ethnographic field site. The course combines a set of standard in-class lectures and tutorials with an 8-12 day field study trip to a location typically outside Hong Kong. The field study trip will consist of both supervised student-led field research and formal face-to-face teaching including such things as guest lectures with local experts, formal professor-guided class discussions on methodology and anthropological fieldwork, guided museum tours, and local study tours focused on the cultural, political, and economic lives of local people. Students will form small groups to investigate different anthropological topics within the field site, actually “doing” anthropology!

Open only to anthropology majors or minors, including minors in archaeology and in cultural heritage studies.

The contents of this course will vary with different instructors and students. Offerings under the same course code, but with different field sites can be taken for credit, up to a maximum of two times.
courses.learning_outcomes:
Upon completion of this course students will:

1) have developed practical fieldwork skills in a real-world environment

2) be able to understand more fully the complexities of fieldwork

3) be able to understand more fully how to collect real-world ethnographic data and how these should be anthropologically presented and written up

4) have a deeper understanding of cross-cultural communication and an in-depth experience with a particular culture.
courses.course_syllabus:
Field sites and topics will vary depending on the Professor offering and accompanying students on the field trip. See Syllabus below.

Because each field study will significantly differ in its particulars, it is impossible to offer a full syllabus. However, each course offered will follow the broad principles:

Anthropological Field Study will have

1) Pre-field study preparation involving three – eight weeks (depending on whether the course is to be offered during the Fall / Spring term or during the Summer Session) of lectures, tutorials, and reading requirements. The field study itself, involving 8-12 days of ethnographic fieldwork, will be closely overseen by the course instructor and will include up to three hours per day of formal classroom instruction which will add up to no less than 12 hours for the trip as a whole.

2) A group report, a final paper, and some form of knowledge-transfer.

A tentative weekly schedule is as follows:

Week 1: Introduction

Week 2: Principles of Ethnography

Week 3: Anthropological Field Methods

Week 4 – 8: Site - Specific Topics (Students will begin to select topics for their own group research during the field trip here as well)

Week 9 – 12: Will be held in the field site (12 hours of formal contact over the course of the 8-12 days of the field trip)

Week 13: Presentations and Final Case Analysis

The 8 - 12 day schedule at the field site will generally follow the following rough outline:

Day 1: Arrival and introduction; meetings with local students and instructor(s) at destination (Destination: To be decided each time offered)

Day 2: Site visits; group interviews; participant observation on selected research topics

Day 3: Visit to local cultural sites and attractions; site visits; group interviews; participant observation on selected research topics

Day 4: Site visits; group interviews; participant observation on selected research topics

Day 5: Guest lectures and workshops; site visits; group interview; participant observation on selected research topics

Day 6: Site visits; group interviews; participant observation on selected research topics

Day 7: Visit to local cultural sites and attractions; site visits; group interviews; participant observation on selected research topics

Day 8: Site visits; group interviews; participant observation on selected research topics

Day 9: Guest lectures and workshops; site visits; group interviews; participant observation on selected research topics

Day 10: Site visits; group interviews; participant observation on selected research topics

Day 11: Group presentations, larger course-level group analyses and discussions, and wrap up

Day 12: Departure and returning to Hong Kong

courses.title: Seminars in the Anthropology of China
courses.description: In this course, students will read some recent ethnographic writing about China. We will come to understand China from a wide variety of perspectives and grapple with questions of the power and limitations of social anthropology to illuminate Chinese society. The weeks will be organized according to topics, but students should remember that ethnographic writing tends to be holistic, so that the author of a given ethnography may use the “topic” of the book as a lens through which she or he explores a wide variety of issues.

• Understand Chinese Society from many perspectives
• Understand how ethnographic research methods vary with the topic addressed
• Understand ethnography as a genre of writing

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Anthropology of Gender, Sexuality and the Law
courses.description:
Advisory: Students are required to have taken at least one course related to gender.

This course will be a cross-cultural and historical study of the contexts in which gender and sexuality are articulated and contested in law. Premised on a social constructivist understanding of gender and sexuality, the course aims to provide a set of tools for students to understand and analyze the norms and frameworks regulating human sexuality through the law. The course further locates the making of gender and sexuality in the law within histories of colonialism and imperialism. Students will learn to evaluate different legislative and judicial responses to issues directly related to sexuality such as consent, rape and adultery, prostitution and human trafficking, violence against women, homosexuality, same-sex and heterosexual marriage etc. They will also learn to examine how legal regulation of gender and sexuality extends into other areas of the law about urban space, inheritance, citizenship, immigration and asylum, as well as the prison system. The course aims at providing students with the critical tools to analyze the cultural and historical constructions that inform “laws in the books, laws in the mind, and laws in action.”

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Making Places: Landscapes, Culture and Society
courses.description:
Landscape is a reflection of past interactions between people and their physical environment, which cumulatively create highly recognizable and culturally distinctive places. Such unique and geographically-defined records of particular groups and their way of life are what UNESCO calls “cultural landscapes” (Rössler 2006). Landscapes also reflect and embody intangible beliefs and if we are to understand such ‘non-material’ meanings we must embrace both Western and non-Western (e.g. Chinese) approaches to their study. Hong Kong’s cultural landscape is overwhelmingly urban and modern in character, embedded within, beyond and beneath the city lie other ‘hidden’ landscapes reflecting more ancient belief systems and traditional practices such as agrarian and maritime lifeways and their ‘traditional’ belief systems. Also, Hong Kong has many culturally important ‘ephemeral’ landscapes, relating to the temporary transformation of spaces, for example during religious festivals, or even the more routine transformations that occur at street eateries (dai pai dong) or markets.

This course explores the concept “landscape”, its tangible and intangible dimensions, how they are physically evidenced locally and abroad, and how anthropologists, archaeologists and a myriad of other disciplines approach their study and interpretation. In particular, we will work through a series of local case studies to see what landscape can tell us about the lifeways, economies, politics and beliefs of past and present communities in Hong Kong. By studying cultural landscapes we can also identify what past and present communities, organisations and governments chose to keep and protect and what they let go – by assessing such processes we can develop an understanding of the underlying socio-political and economic drivers at work through time. In terms of heritage management, therefore, if we wish to militate against the gradual loss of meaning and value in our cultural landscapes, a landscape approach is indicated.

• Concept, history, use and understanding of “landscape” in Western and non-Western contexts

• Landscape as a bridge between disciplines and facilitator of new dialogues

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Archaeological Field Methods
courses.description:
Advisory: ANTH1710 is preferred and priority will be given to students who had taken ANTH1710.

This course is an introduction to archaeological field methods and techniques based on lectures, discussion, and small group practicum classes. The course will start with developing relevant computing skills, the use of reference collections, and the analysis of raw data, as an integral part of the basic tool-kit of archeological field work. Topics of the course will include:

• survey techniques, including augering and field walking;• excavation strategies and recording, including planning and photography;• conservation of archaeological remains or features during excavation;• sampling strategies for dating evidence and other environmental analyses;• post-excavation, report-writing, publication and archiving.
courses.learning_outcomes:
After the course, students will have acquired basic training in archaeological field work methodology and skills covering the following domains:

1. An overview of the methodological issues surrounding archaeological fieldwork.

2. An understanding of various survey techniques.

3. Practical skills for excavation and record-taking.

4. An understanding of aims and methods of scientific analysis employed during the fieldwork.

5. An understanding of the process of designing a project from initial survey to final publication.

Students will also have:

1. developed the tool-kits that are necessary and required in archaeological field work;
2. improved group work skills;
3. acquired experience of academic research, writing and referencing in archaeology.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Visual Anthropology
courses.description: This course explores the history of the moving image in anthropological inquiry. Its primary focus is on the analysis and interpretation of ethnographic films, both the classics as well as non-fiction films with ethnographic value. Students will have the opportunity to do a visual project.
courses.learning_outcomes: In this course students will learn how to analyze and critique cultural representations in general, and visual representations in particular. Because the course focuses on ethnographic and non-fiction films, students will learn to analyse processes of knowledge production. Students will get acquainted with major theories in visual anthropology, as well as the canon of classic ethnographic films. Students will explore the theoretical and methodological issues of the field from a different angle than is usually provided in text-based classes. And finally, students will learn how to think and communicate anthropological ideas visually.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Medicine, Health and Culture
courses.description: This course will focus on the intersection between culture and biology, and introduces major cultural concepts and theories on medicine and health. Starting with an overview of the development of medical knowledge and health care, and the role of society and culture in formulating theories and myths of sickness and healing, the course will examine issues such as culture-bound syndromes and cross-cultural stress and psychiatry; ritual, religious beliefs, and medicine; anthropological perspectives on epidemiology, pharmacology, and doctor-patient relationships; Chinese and Western medical systems; and health and inequality across ethnicity, class and gender. Students are encouraged to think critically about the interaction between biological, environmental and social factors in health and illness, and, as the world becomes more globalized, the integration of alternative medical systems in culturally diverse environments, as well as global health.
courses.learning_outcomes:
At the completion of this course students will:

1) be familiar with, and able to apply, the basic theoretical approaches and methods used in medical anthropology;
2) demonstrate an understanding of the wide range of factors – biological, cultural and environmental – which together shape the health status of individuals and communities, and

3) be familiar with a range of beliefs about health and disease, healing practices and approaches to health in different cultures.
courses.course_syllabus:
This course is an introduction to the field of medical anthropology and explores issues of health, healing, disease and illness in a range of cultures, including your own. Different forms of social and cultural analysis will be applied to a range of local and regional case studies and students will gain an understanding of the key theoretical approaches to the anthropological study of medical knowledge, systems and practices.

The role of medical practitioners and healers, and the political and socio-economic processes shaping the health of individuals and communities, including how ethnicity and gender shape disease profiles and illness experience, are examined. A key focus is on global inequalities in relation to health status, access and the affordability of health care.

Running through the course is the in-depth investigation of illness experiences and help seeking in contemporary China where belief in Chinese medicine, biomedicine and regional healing practices co-exist. These practices are explored in light of the roles of local healers, family care giving and the different ways in which the body, birth, death and illness are managed. The explanatory role of Chinese medicine, local therapies, religion and culturally defined concepts of risk, vulnerability and fate in understanding sickness and healing is explored.

Assessment:

Oral Presentation

Briefing Paper

Updated assessment will be announced in class.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: The Cultures of Cities
courses.description: This course will introduce anthropological approaches to urban studies. Topics to be explored include theories of the origin and development of cities, urbanity in different cultures, urban life and social organization, and problems of urbanization such as adjustment of rural migrants to city life.
courses.learning_outcomes: At the end of this course, students are expected to understand the general concerns in the study of urban anthropology, be able to understand urban life in the framework of global and transnational forces, know how to record and analyze individuals’ urban experience.
courses.course_syllabus:
Hong Kong is Asia’s world city. Posters in the streets remind us to “live it, sense it, and feel it.” This course is designed to introduce anthropological approaches to urban studies. By the end of this course we can find ways to “understand it”.

This course takes the ethnographic perspective to see urban in the light of globalization and transnationalization. It will also take a comparative perspective to understand China’s urban experience in the cross cultural context. Topics to be explored include the origin and development of cities, cities’ new role in the timespace compressed global system, migration, public health, citizenship, social movements, and problems of urbanization such as urban poverty, gender inequality, and social inequality.

The course is open to BA and MA students. Basic anthropology background is not required. Students are expected to read the required reading material before the class. The class lecture will compare the Chinese urban experience with that of the

other cultures.

A research paper is required by the end of the semester. Each student needs to interview a new comer of HK, describe the new immigrant’s experience within the framework learned from the class, and compare his/her experience to the other case

studies mentioned in the class. A one-page proposal of the interview project needs to be submitted around the mid-term time. The proposal should include a brief description of the informant, the interview topic/focus, and the problems you have

encountered in collecting the information.

Take-home mid-term: 30%

Take-home final: 30%

Interview Project: 30%

Participation: 10%

Most updated assessment will be announced in class.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Archaeology of Food
courses.description: Why study past diets? The study of past human diet and nutrition is a key area of research in archaeology and anthropology and holds significant potential for developing a better understanding of human nutrition today. Our eating habits, biologically and culturally, are often rooted in ancient traditions of past millennia but may also reflect recent changes to society and the environment. Through lectures, discussion groups, and practical lab experiences, this course will provide students with advanced knowledge of the main theoretical and methodological approaches to studying nutrition in the ancient past. Major focuses will include stable isotope analyses, zooarchaeology, and archaeobotany.
courses.learning_outcomes:
By the end of this course, students will:

* Gain an appreciation for the deep history of diverse food systems around the world.
* Garner a broad understanding of the major trends and theoretical frameworks related to food-related research in archaeology.
* Demonstrate a firm understanding of basic isotopic, zooarchaeological, and paleoethnobotanical techniques and how they can be used to analyse and interpret archaeological data.
* Critique isotopic, faunal, and botanical data presented in archaeological literature

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Seminars in Hong Kong Studies
courses.description: This course surveys the literature and research topics related to the socio-cultural aspects of urban and rural Hong Kong, including the farming villages in the New Territories and the fishing communities on the off-shore islands.
courses.enrollment_requirement: For students in MPhil Anthropology or MA Anthropology
courses.learning_outcomes:
The course will enable the students to:
• Appreciate and understand the context of urban and rural Hong Kong from historical, cultural, architectural as well as heritage conservation perspectives.
• Learn about the major ethnographic researches on the New Territories
• Apply anthropological theories to apprehend the various historical and socio-cultural aspects of Hong Kong.
• Gain experience in conducting fieldworks in traditional village settlements and folk culture.
courses.course_syllabus:
Hong Kong is always projected as a world-class metropolis and mercantile centre. However, a number of historic Chinese village settlements as well as customs and rituals are still well retained in the New Territories. Such cultural legacy, whether in
the form of tangible or intangible cultural heritage, is diverse and dynamic.

This course aims to explore the socio-cultural context of the New Territories from anthropological, historical, architectural and heritage conservation perspectives. Students will learn to appreciate the distinctiveness and diversity of cultural setting in
the New Territories with an interdisciplinary approach. Fieldtrips will be arranged to enable students to attain a more concrete idea and in-depth understanding of the topics covered in this course. Students are required to attend all the lectures and fieldtrips of this course.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Gender in Asia
courses.description: This course focuses on gender in the Asian region. A comparative approach will be taken to reflect diversity and resemblance continuity and discontinuity, and historical and contemporary influences on gender within countries in the Asian region. Societies studied may vary from year to year, and may include Hong Kong, mainland China, India, Japan, Korea, the Philippines, Taiwan, and Chinese across societies. Gender issues and conditions will be examined within different contexts, covering such areas as language, class, work, family and kinship, health, sexuality, education, religion, development, and politics. Students will read the primary literature and will be expected to write a research paper.
courses.course_syllabus: This course provides students a socio-cultural, transnational and feminist perspective on understanding gender, body and sexuality in a globalizing Asia. Through studying cases from different parts of Asia, such as Hong Kong, China, Taiwan, Japan, Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia, Philippines, Thailand and India, this course will examine the construction of gender through studying how individuals’ bodies and sexualities are subject to kinship, state gender ideology, modernity, migration and globalization. The unifying theme is to examine the relationship between individuals and society – how individuals, situated in a globalizing context, embody gender in their everyday life, AND how society is gendered through individuals’ everyday practices.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Seminars in the Anthropology of China I
courses.description: Students in this course will read and discuss the major ethnographies and other anthropological studies on China. Readings will provide students with general knowledge of the anthropology of China, but will vary year to year depending on the teacher.
courses.enrollment_requirement: For students in PhD Anthropology, MPhil Anthropology or MA Anthropology
courses.learning_outcomes: After following this course, students will have a good knowledge of the study of China by anthropologists, and will be able to pursue their own readings in this field. They will be familiar with the major works and the major topics studied as well as the anthropologists who have done research in China.
courses.course_syllabus:
This course aims to introduce postgraduate students to the anthropological study of China and Chinese culture. The topics that will be discussed include:
1. Introduction: Anthropology of China and Anthropology of Chinese Cultures
2. Community Studies and History of Anthropology in China
3. The Chinese Nation
4. Ethnicity and Identity
5. Lineage, Local Communities and Regions
6. Worldview and Social Relations
7. Religious Life
8. Marriage, Family and Gender
9. Post-Mao Socio-economic Change
10. Memory, Resistance and Political Development
11. Review: Anthropological study of China

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Culture and Mind
courses.description: How can we understand the minds of other people? Do people in different cultures or societies feel and think in different ways? How do childhood experiences affect people and shape or even determine what kinds of persons they will become? What is it like to be mentally abnormal or even pathological? Do people in different cultures or societies experience, understand, and treat psychopathology in different ways? This course examines psychological experiences—feelings, perceptions, thoughts, and motivations—from social and cross-cultural perspectives. It sets out to explore the intersection between anthropology, a field that typically turns to the exotic other, and psychology, a field that often takes the universality of mental activities and mechanisms for granted. Specific focus is placed upon how ethnographers, clinicians, and researchers with training in both fields grapple with various mental phenomena and different ways of understanding them. As most of the materials are drawn from psychological anthropology, this course also serves as an eclectic introduction to this subfield, which was once influential in the history of American anthropology.
courses.learning_outcomes:
1. Students will acquire solid knowledge of cross-cultural comparisons of psychological experiences and their understandings.

2. Students will gain comprehension of the key debates about the universality and relativity of human emotions and individual behavior.

3. Students will think more critically, and develop practical skills and knowledge, about how to understand the minds of other people who are either from the same culture or society or not.

4. Students will achieve comprehension of the major ideas in psychological anthropology, the development in this field and the relationship of psychological anthropology to the general discipline of cultural anthropology.
courses.course_syllabus:
This course introduces students to the studies of psychological experiences from social and cross-cultural perspectives. It examines the intersection between anthropology and psychology, with a specific focus on how ethnographers, clinicians, and researchers with training in both fields grapple with various mental phenomena and different ways of understanding them.

Week 1. Introduction

The course is divided into three parts. The first part “Depth Psychology and Its Cultural Formulations” begins with the Freudian psychoanalysis and its discovery of the unconscious, which has almost become the hallmark of the modern mind. This is followed by a discussion on the encounter of psychoanalysis with 19th-century anthropology that has resulted in imaginative meditations on culture and civilization.

Week 2. The Discovery of the Unconscious

Week 3. Is Oedipus Complex Universal?

Week 4. Culture as Collective Neurosis

Week 5. Civilization and Its Effects

The second part “Culture and Personality and Beyond” deals with some of the most serious endeavors to explore the minds of non-western cultures and societies from the side of anthropology, with a particular focus on the “culture and personality” school that once dominated American anthropology in the middle of the 20th century. The most important strands of studies that derived from it, including comparative childhood studies, phenomenology, and ethnopsychology, are also introduced here.

Week 6. From Configurations to National Characters

Week 7. Cultural and Personality with a Psychoanalytic Bent

Week 8. Comparative Childhood Studies

Week 9. Phenomenology and Ethno-psychology

The last part of the course “The Abnormal Mind” shifts the focus to psychopathology. It begins with culture-bound syndromes that once flourished in the literature of transcultural psychiatry, followed by an extended discussion on the psychotic condition—a fundamental human mental process—and its institutional treatment, and ends with the latest efforts in anthropology to explore the individual mind in society.

Week 10. Culture-Bound Syndromes

Week 11. The Psychotic Mind

Week 12. The Asylum

Week 13. Explorations of Subjectivity

Most updated assessment will be announced in class.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Medicine, Health and Culture
courses.description: This course examines health, illness, and care from a cultural perspective, serving as an introduction to medical anthropology. Students will learn about medical traditions, technologies, and practices in different parts of the world. We will ask and debate many complex questions: How does culture shape the representations and experiences of illness? Is modern medicine also cultural? Why do people choose a treatment from alternative medical traditions, even if these traditions are not “evidence-based”? How does the rise of medical technologies influence social relations such as kinship as well as our views on health, biology, race, and beauty? How did the idea of health as a personal responsibility come about? We will also direct our attention to the culture, economy, and politics of modern medicine by examining the ideologies of science and technology. We will discuss the role of governments, pharmaceutical companies, as well as one’s citizenship, class, gender, and race in experiences of health and suffering, provision of care, and access to medical resources. Weekly lectures will cover a broad range of topics from childhood diseases, reproduction, technologies, organ trafficking, DNA ancestry testing, racism, diabetes, alternative medicine, and the Big Pharma. The themes of health inequality, structural violence, global health, and mental health will be central to class discussions throughout the course. (Not for students who have taken ANT2325.)
courses.learning_outcomes:
By the end of this course, students will be able to:

* describe the history and major theoretical orientations of medical anthropology
* explain the diversity of health-related beliefs, systems of medical knowledge, and practices across different cultures and societies
* analyze the interactions between biological, cultural, and social factors in the shaping of health-related experiences
* analyze the structures of political and economic power that influence the availability, affordability, and desirability of medical resources
* apply the knowledge acquired from readings and class discussions to the analysis of real-world situations, such as genetic testing, medical pluralism, phramaceuticalization, and medical knowledge production
courses.course_syllabus:
* *Week 1: Introduction to the Course**

* This week introduces medical anthropology as a field, including its main perspectives such as a biocultural perspective and critical medical anthropology. The lecture will address the question of how culture, belief, and power shape experiences of health and illness. Readings establish key theoretical frameworks and debates, including how “belief” is understood within biomedicine and cross-cultural medical systems.

* *Week 2: Beginnings and Endings**

* We will examine how societies understand and manage the beginnings and endings of life, from childhood illness to aging, dying, and death. Ethnographic cases highlight how vulnerability and moral responsibility are shaped by social, cultural, and political contexts. They also highlight how people understand and reinterpret medical diagnoses to affirm their agency and how they navigate care within limited settings.

* *Week 3. Sexuality, Gender, and Medicine**

* This week explores how sexuality, reproduction, and gendered bodies are shaped through medical technologies and practices. The lecture will highlight how mainstream medical discourse produces highly gendered accounts of people's bodies and illnesses, and how people navigate the ideals of masculinity and femininity when they are sick. Readings address infertility, reproductive labor, sexual health interventions, and the cultural meanings attached to gendered bodies.

* *Week 4. Ups and Downs of Living**

* Focusing on stress, suffering, and bodily resistance, this week analyzes how social inequalities and everyday pressures become embodied. It also explores how certain conditions like anorexia or smoking become understood by people as integral to their identity, and how this leads to the refusal of treatment. In other words, the assigned ethnographies show how illness, addiction, and distress are lived, resisted, and governed in different social settings.

* *Week 5. The Rise of Biomedical Knowledge as Science**

* In this week we will critically examine biomedicine as both a scientific and symbolic system, questioning the very notion of “science” and “culture.” Readings explore the authority of medical professionals, the rituals of clinical practice, and the cultural meanings attached to scientific knowledge.

* *Week 6. Race and Health Inequalities**

* We will explore the notions of race, racialization, and embodiment, investigating how inequality and historical injustice become embodied as biological difference. Case studies examine structural violence, organ transplantation, and biomedical research to show how social categories produce unequal health outcomes.

* *Week 7. Finding Care in a Changing World**

* This week focuses on how people seek and provide care amid technological change, mobility, and globalization. Readings explore digital health, transnational care networks, and the moral and practical challenges of accessing care across borders. We will highlight how generational and kinship relations, as well as gendered duties of care are reshaped by migration and digital technologies. We will further see how new identities and communities (biosocialities) emerge from the online interactions of people sharing similar medical conditions.

* *Week 8. Alternative Medicine and the Politics of Choice**

* We analyze medical pluralism and the politics of choice between biomedical and alternative healing systems. Ethnographies highlight how patients navigate authority, expertise, family traditions, and global flows of medical knowledge. We will address why and how people make choices across available treatments, and how doctors of alternative medicine see their profession amid the contested politics of knowledge.

* *Week 9. Genes and Technology**

* This week examines how genetic and biomedical technologies reshape understandings of kinship, risk, responsibility, and identity across cultural contexts. Through cases such as direct-to-consumer genetic testing, epigenetics, and reproductive technologies, the readings show how biological knowledge is socially produced and unevenly distributed. We also explore the ethical tensions and social consequences that arise as genetic explanations intersect with existing inequalities, family relations, and global health priorities.

* *Week 10. Medicalization, Phramaceuticalization, and Agency**

* We explore how different aspects of existence have become medicalized, i.e. viewed as medical conditions requiring treatment rather than expected life events. We will also talk about food, beauty, and wellbeing becoming pharmaceuticalized, and how patients exercise agency navigating these processes. Case studies address chronic illness, drug markets, and the global circulation of medications.

* *Week 11. Understanding Wellness and Metal Health**

* This week focuses on mental health, wellness, and therapeutic practices across cultural contexts. We will question what wellness means for different people and, what is viewed as “normal” and “pathological” in different communities. Readings examine mindfulness, addiction, and psychiatric care, emphasizing how suffering and healing are culturally produced and contested.

* *Week 12. Life amid Political and Environmental Disasters**

* This week examines how human-made and environmental disasters shape health, suffering, and survival in contexts of ecological change, war, and political violence. Readings from the Anthropocene and conflict settings explore how environmental degradation, fear, trauma, and loss become embodied, revealing unequal exposure to harm and uneven possibilities for recovery. Together, the ethnographies highlight how states, institutions, and global forces determine who is protected, who is neglected, and how life is valued or allowed to deteriorate in times of crisis.

* *Week 13. Globalization, Media, and the Future**

* The final week examines the global circulation of biomedical practices and humanitarian interventions. Readings reflect on the future of medical anthropology, addressing global health emergencies, media, and emerging forms of inequality and care.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: From Madness to Mental Health
courses.description: This course examines mental illness and mental health as subjective experiences, social processes, and objects of scientific knowledge and practice. It invites students to explore human experiences that are labelled as abnormal or pathological, to understand the expert knowledge and technologies employed to remedy these conditions, and to think about the complex relationships between them and the broader social and cultural contexts. Readings are drawn from psychiatric anthropology or anthropology of mental health, clinical case studies, and memoirs. They are chosen to reflect an interdisciplinary scope that includes social sciences, psychiatry itself, and the layman’s/patient’s perspective.
courses.learning_outcomes:
Our goal is that after taking this course, you will have:

1. Acquired basic knowledge in psychiatric anthropology or anthropology of mental health.

2. Developed a sophisticated understanding of psychiatry as a cultural domain and a social institution as well as a critical concern for mental health as a social issue.

3. Gained foundational knowledge regarding the symptomatology and illness experiences of major mental illnesses.

4. Become conversant in a range of ethnographic examples of how mental illness and mental health interact with local social and cultural contexts.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Magic, Myth and the Supernatural
courses.description: This course will examine phenomena often viewed as irrational and superstitious to see how they can be understood in cultural terms. All societies have some belief in another world, yet beliefs vary widely between societies. The course will examine traditional anthropological topics such as magic, traditional healing, divination, fengshui, witchcraft, and ghosts, as well as more recent issues such as ESP, psychokinesis, qigong, vampires, zombies, monsters, UFOs and alien abduction. The role of myth in modern society and the cultural creation of reality will be highlighted. The power of a cultural approach in explaining the supernatural and the limits of what science can explain will also be discussed. Students will read the primary literature and will be expected to write a research paper.
courses.course_syllabus:
This course will examine phenomena often viewed as irrational and superstitious to see how they can be understood in cultural terms. All societies have some belief in another world, yet beliefs vary widely between societies. The course will examine the truth-value of many beliefs (are there vampires and UFOs?), but will focus especially on understanding why humans hold “unscientific” beliefs and how they make sense in cultural terms. The course will examine traditional
anthropological topics such as magic, traditional healing, divination, fengshui, witchcraft, and ghosts, as well as more recent issues such as ESP, psychokinesis, qigong, vampires, zombies, monsters, UFOs and alien abduction. The role of myth in modern society and the cultural creation of reality will be highlighted. Examples from contemporary industrial societies, especially the United States and Hong Kong, will be used to challenge notions of “modern (or Western) rationality” as well as “traditional superstition.” The power of a cultural approach in explaining the supernatural and the limits of what science can explain will also be discussed.

Readings for this course are from non-specialist magazines and specially selected for a General Education course; all university-educated adults should be able to read these kinds of articles. Students should do the readings before class, especially those students who feel their English is weak. The readings will help you learn the vocabulary of the lecture. You are also expected to contribute to the discussion in class and in the tutorial. (The “Participation” component of the grade is not a grade of how brilliant comments are, but only whether you participate or not—by asking and answering questions, making comments, etc.)

Outlines of the lectures (the PowerPoint slides) will be posted at least one day before the lecture on Moodle at http://moodle.cuhk.edu.hk Note that the illustrations are removed in cases where I do not have copyright (but can be used in class for educational purposes). Any updates for the course will also be posted there.
courses.required_readings:
(Most updated reading list will be announced in class.)

All readings have been placed on reserve in the University Library. For articles in edited volumes, be sure to search for chapters by the book title or book editor's name, not by author's name. Please note that there are multiple editions of the following books, and the articles may be only in some editions:
Lehmann, Arthur C., and James E. Myers, eds. 1993 and 2001 Magic, Witchcraft, and Religion: An Anthropological Study of the Supernatural (3rd edition and 5th edition).
Spradley, James, & James McCurdy 2003 Conformity and Conflict.
Other recommended readings will be suggested in class and on the Moodle page.

Topics:

Introduction No tutorials this week.

Magic
1) Gmelch, George “Baseball Magic.” In Lehmann and Myers 5th edition (a revised version) (Also in Spradley & McCurdy 2003, pp. 348-357). [A famous article that discusses magic in sports and introduces the anthropological analysis of magic across cultures.]
2) Carey, Benedict. 2007. “Do You Believe in Magic?” The New York Times. http://www.nytimes.com/2007/01/23/health/psychology/23magic.html

Urban Legends and Rumors
1) Brunvand, Jan Harold 1981 Chapters 1 & 3 in The Vanishing Hitchhiker: American Urban Legends and Their Meanings, pp. 1-16, 47-69. [An introduction to urban legends and some famous examples from the USA.]

Ghosts and Spirits
1) Evans, Grant “Ghosts and the New Governor: The Anthropology of a Hong Kong Rumor.” In Grant Evans and Maria Tam Siu-mi, eds. Hong Kong: The Anthropology of a Chinese Metropolis, pp. 267-296. [This is an analysis of the case of the ghost(s) in the 1992 KCR commercial.]
2) Freed, Stanley A. and Ruth S. Freed “Taraka’s Ghost” in Lehmann and Myers (3rd ed.) pp. 287-291. (Also in Spradley & McCurdy 2003 Conformity and Conflict, pp. 341-347). [This is a famous Indian example of possession by a ghost.]

Divination
1) Hyman, Ray “Cold Reading: How to Convince Strangers That You Know All About Them.” In Kendrick Frazier, ed. Paranormal Borderlands of Science, pp. 79-96. [A key article that explains how fortune-telling works]
2) Rapport, Nigel. 1988. "A Policeman's Construction of 'The Truth': Sergeant Hibbs and the Lie-Detector Machine." Anthropology Today 4(1):7-11 (available from the ULI online through JSTOR) [This article shows how the "lie detector" machine is a form of divination. Keep in mind as you read this article that the lie detector is not reliable (though it claims to be scientific), and that the result of the test itself is not admissible in court, though if the suspect confesses to the operator, that confession is admissible.]

Witchcraft and Evil Eye
1) Burke, Charlanne. "Witchcraft Tswana Style." In James Spradley and David McCurdy Conformity and Conflict 11th Edition, pp. 358-370. [An example of contemporary witchcraft in Africa].
2) Luhrmann, Tanya. "The Goat and the Gazelle: Witchcraft." In William A. Haviland and Robert J. Gordon, eds. Talking About People: Readings in Contemporary Cultural Anthropology (1993 edition), pp.232-239. [An example of modern witchcraft in
England]

Shamanism
1) Howells, William “The Shaman: A Siberian Spiritualist.” In Lehmann and Myers (all editions) [This article describes the classic example of shamanism.]
2) Harner, Michael. 2003 (orig. 1980). "Discovering the Way." In Harvey, Graham, ed. 2003. Shamanism: A Reader. New York: Routledge, pp. 41-56. [Harner describes how he was initiated into the practice of shamanism. A good example of the complex
combination of pharmacology, cosmology, psychology and sociology of shamanism.]

Midterm. No tutorial for this week.

Traditional healing
1) Dubisch, Jill “You are What You Eat: Religious Aspects of the Health Food Movement.” In Lehmann and Myers (3rd ed. pp. 55-63; 5th edition pp. 73-81). [This article shows how whether something is viewed as "health food" in the US is as much determined by our symbolic system for classifying foods as by biomedical facts.]
2) Dodes, John E. 1997 “The Mysterious Placebo.” Skeptical Inquirer 21(1):44-5 (avail. online). [This brief article explains the placebo effect, or how just thinking you are taking a medicine can make you better.]

Vampires and Monsters
1) Barber, Paul “The Real Vampire” in Lehmann and Myers (3rd ed. pp. 307-312) (5th ed. 318-323). [The author discovers that the original stories of vampires in Eastern Europe are based on how the body decomposes. Do not read right after eating!]
Evans, Grant 1993 "Bringing the mermaid myth back to port." (SCMP handout) [A short newspaper article about a rumor about a mermaid in 1993 Hong Kong. Why does the author have to write back to the SCMP after they cut the last paragraph of his article?]
2) Jones, David E. 2000 Chapter 7 "Fate of the Dragons" in An Instinct for Dragons pp. 113-119. [The author asks why all cultures have dragons, and why we fear dragons. Do you agree with the author?]

Myths
1) Campbell, Joseph, 1988 first half of Chapter 5 "The Hero's Adventure" in The Power of Myth (with Bill Moyers) pp. 123-140 in large-format version (pp. 151-172 in small font 1991 edition of the book with few illustrations). [This chapter, from a popular book and video (also available at the UC video library) discusses the hero in myth.]
2) Leonard, Scott, and Michael McClure. 2008 (orig. 2004). “The Study of Mythology.” In Moro, Myers and Lehmann, eds. Magic, Witchcraft and Religion (7th edition) pp.51-62. [This text, originally from an introduction to a book about myths, lays out the
different approaches to the mythology, the study of myth.]

UFOs and Alien Abduction
1) Huston, Peter. 1992. "Night Terrors, Sleep Paralysis, and Devil Stricken Telephone Cords From Hell." Skeptical Inquirer 17(1):64-68 (avail. online). Also in Kendrick Frazier, ed. 1998. Encounters with the Paranormal pp. 294-299. [A short article on vivid images we have as we fall asleep and as we wake up.]
2) Whitmore, John. 2008 (orig. 1995). “Religious Dimensions of the UFO Abductee Experience.” In Moro, Myers and Lehmann, eds. Magic, Witchcraft and Religion (7th edition) pp. 418-27.

Conclusion: "Superstition," Relativism, and Science
1) Sagan, Carl “The Burden of Skepticism” in Lehmann and Myers (3rd ed. pp. 371-376) (5th ed. pp. 384-389). [The late Carl Saga, an astrophysicist, discusses why we must be skeptical, but not be cynical or closed-minded.]
2) Lewis, I. M. “The Anthropologist’s Encounter with the Supernatural.” In Lehmann and Myers (3rd ed.) pp. 18-23. [The author, an anthropologist, argues that we can never conclusively exclude the possibility of supernatural beings.]

Final Exam: to be centrally scheduled.
