courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Religion and Culture
courses.description: Religious practices and beliefs permeate most aspects of culture throughout the world and religion has always been one of the most important topics in anthropology and liberal studies. This course examines the following aspects of religion: magic & sorcery, symbolism & ritual, gender and religion, shamanism, syncretism, and social change driven by religious ideas. The course also introduces major traditions of social theory: each tradition offers a different way of looking at the role of religion in people's lives. This course thus introduces students to various forms of religious expression around the world and also exposes them to different interpretations of religion. MA students will read the primary literature and will be expected to write a research paper.
courses.learning_outcomes:
1. Students will be familiar with the major anthropological theories of religion.
2. Students will learn about the major religions and some indigenous peoples’ beliefs and practices.
3. Students will learn about religious tolerance and avoid religiocentrism.
4. Students will have a greater understanding of religions and human societies.
courses.course_syllabus:
This course aims to introduce students to some anthropological approaches to the study of religions. Students will learn to appreciate the diversity of religions as well as their functions in human societies. In addition, students will learn about the major world religions, as well as Chinese and some other indigenous religious traditions. The significance of religion in present and future human societies will be discussed, too.
Topics
1. Introduction: Definitions and Anthropological Perspectives
2. Diversity and Similarity of Religions
3. Religion and Individuals
4. Religion and Society
5. Buddhism and Societies
6. Christianity and Societies
7. Islam and Societies
8. Chinese Religions and Societies
9. Religious Specialists, Rituals and Symbols
10. Politics and Religion
11. Globalization, Modernization and Religion
12. Religion and Human Future
courses.required_readings:
The readings will be from many sources, but the following texts are useful.
1) Bowie, Fiona. The Anthropology of Religion. Oxford: Blackwell, 2000.
2) Lambek, Michael, ed. A Reader in the Anthropology of Religion. Oxford: Blackwell, 2002.
3) Lessa, William A. and Evon Z. Vogt, eds. Reader in Comparative Religion: An Anthropological Approach. NY: Harper & Row, 1979 (4th ed.)
4) Winzeler, Robert L. Anthropology and Religion: What We Know, Think, and Question. Lanham: AltaMira Press, 2008.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Seminars in General Anthropology
courses.description: This course offers students a chance to explore the various sub-disciplines of anthropology. Students read for one topic each week, and discuss readings in a seminar with a teacher. The readings and discussions help prepare students for the General Anthropology Examination.
courses.learning_outcomes:
After taking this course, students should be able to
a) understand different subfields in anthropology
b) name major theories and perspectives within each field
c) think analytically about the major issues within those subfields and understand the complex linkages among different fields
d) be able to better prepare for the General Anthropology Exam at the end of the MA program
courses.course_syllabus: This course covers the major subfields of cultural anthropology and archeology. Co-taught by all the teachers in the department, the course aims to enhance students’ anthropological knowledge, both the major theories and general anthropology.
courses.required_readings:
Introduction (Wu Keping)

Economic Anthropology (Joseph Bosco)
- - Wilk, Richard R., and Lisa Cliggett. 2007. Economies and Cultures: Foundations of Economic Anthropology (2nd edition). Boulder: Westview. Read Chapters 2-5 & 7).

Paper topic: Use the ideas and theories in the Wilk and Cliggett book to discuss the problem of "greed." For example, are bankers of Wall Street really greedy? Is hyperconsumerism caused by greed? If everyone is "self-interested", what is "greed" anyway? Can we say that there is greed at the individual, social-political and cultural levels discussed in the book? Use the ideas of the book and any examples and other sources to discuss "greed."

Students interested in American popular culture may like to know that the character Gordon Gekko in the 1987 movie "Wall Street" famously said "Greed is good" (see the video clip and text of his speech at www.americanrhetoric.com/MovieSpeeches/moviespeechwallstreet.html ). He is expressing the idea that capitalism only works based on "self-interest." The problem is, Gekko is a cheat and inside trader, not a law-abiding capitalist investor (see the movie synopsis here if you don't want to watch the movie: http://www.imdb.com/title/tt0094291/synopsis ). A writer that is now popular with the "Tea Party", Ayn Rand, also argued that "greed is good." There are many other examples you can pick to discuss.

Language and Communication (Gordon Mathews)
- -Salzman, Zdenak (2004) Language, Culture, and Society: An Introduction to Linguistic Anthropology. Boulder: Westview Press. Read chapters 1-5, 8-11, 13

Paper topic: What is the relation of language to culture and society?

Ethnography (Wang Danning)
- -Lee, Anru. 2004. In The Name of Harmony and Prosperity: Labor and Gender Politics in Taiwan's Economic Restructuring. Albany: State University of New York Press. Chapters 1, 2, 3, 5 and 7.

Paper topic: People work, but what makes them to work varies in different societies and changes in different times. In this Taiwan case, we see the transformation of industrial structure affected the meaning of work, work ethic, family relationship, as well as local people’s understanding of the world. Good ethnographies covered both macro and micro levels of social dynamics. Please use some examples from this particular piece to illustrate how ethnographers can accomplish this in their writings.

Gender (Wang Danning)
- - Bonvillain, Nancy (2001) Women and Men: Cultural Constructs of Gender (3rd edition). Upper Saddle River, NJ: Prentice Hall. Read the entire book with emphasis on Ch 1, 6, 8 and 9.

Paper topic: "The more a society develops, the more unequal its gender relations". Do you agree? Explain with ethnographic examples.

Kinship: Basic Concepts (WU Keping)
- -Stone, Linda. 2006. Kinship and Gender: An Introduction (3rd ed.) Boulder, CO: Westview Press. Ch. 1.
- - Parkin, Robert. 1997. Kinship: An Introduction to the Basic Concepts. Oxford: Blackwell. Ch. 1.
- - Clark W. Sorensen, "Asian Families: Domestic Group Formation." In Asia's Cultural Mosaic: An Anthropological Introduction, ed., Grants Evans, pp. 89-117. NY: Prentice Hall, 1993.

- - Fox, Robin Kinship and Marriage, Ch.2 , “The Incest Problem”
- - Chapais, Bernard. 2008. Primeval Kinship: How Pair-Bonding Gave Birth to Human Society. Cambridge, Mass.: Harvard U Press. Ch. 5., “The Incest Avoidance Legacy”

Paper Topic: Discuss the importance of kinship and marriage in today’s society.

Religion (TAN Chee-Beng)
- -Bowen, John (2002) Religions in Practice: An Approach to the Anthropology of Religion. Boston, Mass: Allyn and Bacon. Chapters1, 2,3,4,15

Paper Topic: Discuss the relevance of religion in today's world using ideas and theories introduced by Bowen.

Political Anthropology (Sidney Cheung)
- -Lewellen, Ted. 2003. Political Anthropology: An Introduction. Westport, CT: Praeger.

Paper Topic: How can political anthropology help to understand today's natural resource management? Use the awarded documentary The Cove to discuss.

Heritage Studies and Archeology (Tracey Lu)
- -Renfrew, Colin, and Paul Bahn. 2004. Archaeology: Theories, Methods and Practice, 4th ed., chapter 5, 12 and 14. London: Thames and Hudson.

Paper Topic: Why is archaeology a discipline of anthropology? Discuss with examples.

Ethnicity: Basic Concepts (CHEN Ju-chen)

Chapters 1, 2, 3

Chapters 6.

Paper Topic: “The study of ethnicity requires the study of the nation-state and vice-versa.” Discuss this statement.

Ethnography (Gordon Mathews)

Paper Topic: Why are Bourgois’s informants drug dealers and addicts? Is it their own fault?

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Understanding Islam
courses.description: This class begins its study of Islam by examining the historical developments of Islam in pre-Islamic Arabia and looking at the life of various religious figures. It then examines aspects of Islamic civilization, culture and philosophy. Finally it addresses issues of the so-called ‘politicization of religion’ in the context of globalizing modernity and violent conflict. Throughout this course we will investigate the insights that anthropological analyses can offer to discussions centering the relations between Muslim societies and the West. Students in this course will engage in in-depth reading and discussion, and will write reports and research papers on aspects of Islam.
courses.learning_outcomes:
• Students will appreciate the contemporary cultural diversity, values and world views of Muslims living in diverse circumstances and places
• Understand the contemporary struggles over religious authority and orthodoxy in some parts of the Muslim world
• Understand the tensions and potential conflicts between religious ideas and practices relating to gender, education and art
• Be able to challenge and think critically about stereotypes about Muslims and Islam

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: The Cultures of Cities
courses.description: This course will introduce anthropological approaches to urban studies. Topics to be explored include theories of the origin and development of cities, urbanity in different cultures, urban life and social organization, and problems of urbanization such as adjustment of rural migrants to city life. MA students will read the primary literature and will be expected to write a research paper. (Not for students who have taken ANT4410.)
courses.learning_outcomes: At the end of this course, students are expected to understand the general concerns in the study of urban anthropology, be able to understand urban life in the framework of global and transnational forces, know how to record and analyze individuals’ urban experience.
courses.course_syllabus:
Hong Kong is Asia’s world city. Posters in the streets remind us to “live it, sense it, and feel it.” This course is designed to introduce anthropological approaches to urban studies. By the end of this course we can find ways to “understand it”.

This course takes the ethnographic perspective to see urban in the light of globalization and transnationalization. It will also take a comparative perspective to understand China’s urban experience in the cross cultural context. Topics to be explored include the origin and development of cities, cities’ new role in the timespace compressed global system, migration, public health, citizenship, social movements, and problems of urbanization such as urban poverty, gender inequality, and social inequality.

The course is open to BA and MA students. Basic anthropology background is not required. Students are expected to read the required reading material before the class. The class lecture will compare the Chinese urban experience with that of the
other cultures.

A research paper is required by the end of the semester. Each student needs to interview a new comer of HK, describe the new immigrant’s experience within the framework learned from the class, and compare his/her experience to the other case
studies mentioned in the class. A one-page proposal of the interview project needs to be submitted around the mid-term time. The proposal should include a brief description of the informant, the interview topic/focus, and the problems you have
encountered in collecting the information.
courses.required_readings:
1) Gmelch, George, and Walter P. Zenner, 2002, Urban Life: Readings in the Anthropology of the City, 4th edition, Waveland Press, Inc.
2) Macionis, John J. and Vincent N. Parrillo. 2007. Cities and Urban Life. 4th edition. NJ: Pearson/Prentice Hall.
3) Sassen, Saskia, 1994, Cities in a World Economy, Thousand Oaks, Pine Forge Press.
These three books have been reserved in the University Library (ULR). Articles that assigned for each week will also be available on Reserve in the University Library (ULR).

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Cultures of Japan and Korea
courses.description: This course provides an anthropological approach to the study of Japan and Korea, with a particular focus on social change and their infl uences on other East Asian countries. This course will concentrate on cultural traditions, lineage, religions, social structure and contemporary international relationships of the two countries. Teaching materials will include ethnographies, popular writings, news features, movies, etc., in order to provide students with a comprehensive approach for understanding the cultures of Japan and Korea. MA students will read the primary literature and will be expected to write a research paper. (Not for students who have taken ANT4460.)
courses.learning_outcomes: Students will be introduced to cultural traditions, lineage, religions, social structure and contemporary international relationships of the two countries. Upon completing the course, students will be able to use the analytical tools they have acquired to understand their own societies. In this sense, the course fulfils the anthropological condition of studying the other in order to better understand the self.
courses.course_syllabus: This class is designed to give you an in-depth understanding of the cultures of Japan and Korea. “Culture” in this course does not refer merely to fine arts, to Japanese ink-painting and Korean dance; rather, it refers to all the ways in which Japanese and Koreans live in the world today. In the first half of the course, we examine values and institutions in Japan and South Korea, looking at the underlying cultural principles of the two societies, and at the ways in which the Japanese and Korean governments and societies use those principles to mold their citizens to live and think in certain ways. We also examine the relation of culture to economics in the two societies, particularly in terms of Japan and South Korea’s extraordinary economic growth over the past four decades, and recent economic difficulties. We also examine high culture and popular culture in the two societies, and the meanings of religion in the two societies. In the second half of the course, we turn to the individual lives of Japanese and Koreans. We examine the relationships of men and women in the two societies, and the meanings of work and family; we consider the social constructions of youth and age, and “the generation gap”; and we consider outsiders and insiders in the two societies, and the two societies’ relationship to the world. This course aims to enable you to better understand the particular societies of Japan and South/North Korea, but also to better be able to anthropologically analyze and compare complex societies throughout the world.
courses.required_readings: Readings from books are available in NA or UL Library. Readings from newspaper articles, as well from several books that are not in the university library, are available in the bookcase opposite the Anthropology Office, from which you may make copies.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Peoples and Cultures of Southeast Asia
courses.description: The primary aim of this course is to introduce peoples and cultures of Southeast Asia through the study of anthropology. The course will highlight cultural similarities and differences and explore the issues of ethnicity, development and national identity.
courses.learning_outcomes: Students will be acquainted with the prehistory, history, geography and the forces of colonialism and post-colonialism in Southeast Asia, all of which will help them understand the current situation in the region. Students will be made to reflect on how social, cultural and political institutions provide lenses for understanding Southeast Asian society. Students will be introduced to current crises confronting the region such as ecological/environmental disasters and religio-political conflicts including terrorism, which have implications for the world at large. Upon completing the course, students will be able to use the analytical tools they have acquired to understand their own societies. In this sense, the course fulfils the anthropological condition of studying the other in order to better understand the self.
courses.course_syllabus:
This course invites you to rethink Southeast Asia by reading from anthropological as well as non-anthropological works. As one of the most economically vibrant regions in the world, it has also attracted the attention of scholars due to its ethnic, religious, political and cultural diversities.

Today, it has become a region which has footed itself firmly on the world map. But is there such a region as “Southeast Asia”? Do Southeast Asians see themselves in regional terms of unity? Or division and diversity? How can you understand Southeast Asia? From whose perspectives? And whose voices? I will conduct this course as a seminar to enable the MA students to debates these issues and in the process use the analytical tools they have acquired to understand their own
societies. In this sense, the course fulfils the anthropological condition of studying the other in order to better understand the self.
courses.required_readings: We will not be using any particular text book in this course as readings will be taken from a number of books which will all be scanned and placed on the course Webpage. This can be accessed through Moodle.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Cultures of Chinese Overseas
courses.description: This course will introduce students to the study of Chinese communities outside China. Ethnic Chinese communities worldwide may be considered as comprising an ethnological field. Due to the sharing of aspects of Chinese civilization, Chinese everywhere share some cultural similarities. However, the need to adapt to different ecological, political and sociocultural environments calls for adaptation and transformation. Thus the diverse Chinese communities worldwide are ideal for comparative studies, especially on a number of anthropological/sociological themes such as cultural continuity and transformation, cultural identities and ethnic identities, ethnic relations, social organization, and so on. Students will read the primary literature and will be expected to write a research paper.
courses.learning_outcomes:
1) To become familiar with Chinese migration and life in different parts of the world
2) To gain appreciation for cultural diversity among Chinese in different parts of the world
3) To understand the nature of transnational networks among Chinese overseas and with China
4) To be aware of not essentializing identities and to respect diverse and multiple ethnic identification
5) To gain a basic knowledge of ethnic Chinese studies for research and teaching
courses.course_syllabus:
In this course you will learn about Chinese communities worldwide. There is much that we can learn from the diverse experiences of migration and settlement of Chinese in different parts of the world. While this is an anthropological course, our readings will be interdisciplinary. The topics that we will discuss include:
1. Introduction: Labels and the Study of Chinese Overseas
2. Migration and Diaspora
3. Chinese Migration: Asia
4. Chinese Migration: The Americas
5. Chinese in Europe and Russia
6. Chinese in Australasia and Africa
7. Localization, Ethnogenesis and Identities
8. Cultural Reproduction and Identity
9. Family, Kinship, Transnational Networks and China
10. Global Capitalism, Transnationalism and China
11. Migration, Remigration and Homelands

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Anthropological Field Study
courses.description:
This course will enable students to extend their anthropological learning in the classroom to an ethnographic field site. The course combines a set of standard in-class lectures and tutorials with an 8-12 day field study trip to a location typically outside Hong Kong. The field study trip will consist of both supervised student-led field research and formal face-to-face teaching including such things as guest lectures with local experts, formal professor-guided class discussions on methodology and anthropological fieldwork, guided museum tours, and local study tours focused on the cultural, political, and economic lives of local people. Students will form small groups to investigate different anthropological topics within the field site.

Open only to anthropology majors.
The contents of this course will vary with different instructors and students. Offerings under the same course code, but with different field sites can be taken for credit, up to a maximum of two times.
courses.learning_outcomes:
Upon completion of this course students will:

1) have developed practical fieldwork skills in a real-world environment
2) be able to understand more fully the complexities of fieldwork
3) be able to understand more fully how to collect real-world ethnographic data and how these should be anthropologically presented and written up
4) have a deeper understanding of cross-cultural communication and an in-depth experience with a particular culture.
courses.course_syllabus:
Field sites and topics will vary depending on the Professor offering and accompanying students on the field trip. See Syllabus below.

Because each field study will significantly differ in its particulars, it is impossible to offer a full syllabus. However, each course offered will follow the broad principles:

Anthropological Field Study will have
1) Pre-field study preparation involving three – eight weeks (depending on whether the course is to be offered during the Fall / Spring term or during the Summer Session) of lectures, tutorials, and reading requirements. The field study itself, involving 8-12 days of ethnographic fieldwork, will be closely overseen by the course instructor and will include up to three hours per day of formal classroom instruction which will add up to no less than 12 hours for the trip as a whole.
2) A group report, a final paper, and some form of knowledge-transfer.

A tentative weekly schedule is as follows: Week 1: Introduction
Week 2: Principles of Ethnography Week 3: Anthropological Field Methods
Week 4 – 8: Site - Specific Topics (Students will begin to select topics for their own group research during the field trip here as well) Week 9 – 12: Will be held in the field site (12 hours of formal contact over the course of the 8-12 days of the field trip)
Week 13: Presentations and Final Case Analysis

The 8 - 12 day schedule at the field site will generally follow the following rough outline:
Day 1: Arrival and introduction; meetings with local students and instructor(s) at destination (Destination: To be decided each time offered) Day 2: Site visits; group interviews; participant observation on selected research topics
Day 3: Visit to local cultural sites and attractions; site visits; group interviews; participant observation on selected research topics Day 4: Site visits; group interviews; participant observation on selected research topics
Day 5: Guest lectures and workshops; site visits; group interview; participant observation on selected research topics Day 6: Site visits; group interviews; participant observation on selected research topics
Day 7: Visit to local cultural sites and attractions; site visits; group interviews; participant observation on selected research topics Day 8: Site visits; group interviews; participant observation on selected research topics
Day 9: Guest lectures and workshops; site visits; group interviews; participant observation on selected research topics Day 10: Site visits; group interviews; participant observation on selected research topics
Day 11: Group presentations, larger course-level group analyses and discussions, and wrap up Day 12: Departure and returning to Hong Kong
courses.required_readings:
Because each field study will be led by a different teacher to a different location, it is impossible to have a common reading list. Each different anthropological field study course will have its own required reading list, based on the region being explored and the topic being investigated. However, there are some books dealing with how to do ethnographic fieldwork in a foreign, real-world setting that will indeed be used in common for all offerings of the course:

Emerson, Robert M., Rachel I. Fretz, and Linda L. Shaw. 2011. Writing Ethnographic Fieldnotes, 2nd Edition. Chicago: University of Chicago Press. Guest , Kenneth J. 2016. Cultural Anthropology Fieldwork Journal. 2nd Edition. New York: W. W.
Norton. Hammersley, Martyn, and Paul Atkinson. 2007. Ethnography: Principles in Practice. 3rd edition. London: Routledge.

Robben, Antonius, and Jeffrey Sluka, eds. 2012. Ethnographic Fieldwork: An Anthropological Reader. 2nd Edition. Cambridge MA: Wiley- Blackwell.

Wolcott, Harry F. 2004. The Art of Fieldwork. 2nd Edition. Lanham MD: Altamira

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Culture and Business
courses.description: This course will examine the role of culture in contemporary business. It will introduce anthropological approaches to the study of work and management in industrial societies. Topics include cross-cultural communication in business settings, business organization (e.g., the Japanese factory, the Chinese family firm), cultural values and the motivation to work, retail marketing and consumer culture, and occupational and company sub-culture.
courses.learning_outcomes:
1. To expand students' understanding and appreciation of the cultural dimensions of business operations and organization in different historical, political, and social settings.
2. To cultivate students' knowledge of ethnographic approaches to the study of diverse aspects of business operations and organization, with an emphasis on participant-observation fieldwork methodologies.
3. To enhance students' comprehension of key anthropological concepts, frameworks, and theories integral to the comparative study and analysis of business enterprises and corporate cultures.
4. To sharpen students' critical reading, listening, and writing skills, particularly their ability to grasp, articulate, synthesize, and challenge arguments and debates in readings, lectures, films, and discussions.
5. To foster students' critical awareness of significant issues concerning business history, culture, and politics in their own society so that they can participate actively and responsibly as local citizens in a globalizing world.
courses.course_syllabus:
Similar as many aspects in our lives, business behavior is now commonly acknowledged as culturally constructed. Even the most influential and popular business entity – the corporate company – was in fact the product of a political battle with profound political, social, and cultural implications. This course is designed to take historical, comparative, and ethnographic perspectives to reveal the social and cultural aspects of running business and the cultural logics of business practices. This
course will also take a cross-cultural perspective to deconstruct the dominant economic rationality to compare business practices in various societies and historical periods.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Political Violence and Human Rights
courses.description: This course examines the problem of violence and its political uses from an anthropological and comparative perspective. The range of phenomena that can be called violent is very broad. We focus here on the state and human rights and the ways various state and non-state actors promote their political goals through violent means. We will also examine the cultural issues involving human rights (such as human rights as a universal value and the issue of cultural relativism) and analyze the discourses and practices of human rights as politics, and what these new forms of political authority may entail. MA students will read the primary literature and will be expected to write a research paper.
courses.course_syllabus:
How is violence used as a political instrument? How and why do governments engage in violent actions against their own citizens? What are human rights? This course examines the problems of violence and its political uses from an anthropological perspective and within a comparative framework. The range of phenomena that can be called violence is very broad and varies greatly across cultures. We focus here on violence as a political problem, and the ways in which various state and non-state actors promote their political goals through violent means, such as torture, terrorism, or genocide. We analyse the relationships between politics and violence, the emergence and use of human rights discourses and practices as a possible political remedy against mass violence, and what new forms of political authority based on human rights may entail. In this course, we will critically analyse global violence issues including genocide in Cambodia and Rwanda, mass rape in Bosnia-Herzegovina and state terror in Colombia. We question why the spread of a human rights culture cannot stop the emergence of violence all over the world. Also, throughout the course, recent human rights issues will be discussed in lectures and tutorials. The course intends to develop students’ critical understanding of everyday violence in our society and at the international level.

Course Structure
Part I: The Human Rights Framework and Theoretical Approaches to Violence
This section introduces the theoretical problems surrounding violence and culture, and uses of violence for political goals by states and non-state actors. The readings introduce the contradictions between political violence and human rights, for instance in torture or terrorism. The issue of human rights cannot be understood without first giving students the tools to understand mass organized violence, i.e. what human rights aim to remedy according to the Charter of the Universal Declaration on Human Rights signed by all member states of the United Nations.

Part II: Human Rights, Universalism and Cultural Relativism
Based on the previous themes of violence and culture, this section introduces the historical and conceptual frameworks for students to analyse the emergence of discourses on human rights. It introduces the debates over the universality of human rights, which is the main source of contention for the rejection of human rights by some governments. Students will be able to analyse the question of political rationality and relativism, and apply arguments for and against the universality of human rights after this section.

Part III: Case Studies on Political Violence
Based on the concepts of violence and human rights introduced in the previous two sections, this section analyses case studies of gross denials of human right through mass violence. These case studies underline the limits of international politics based on human rights. In these case studies of paramilitary terror, genocide, and mass rape and gendered violence against women, human rights failed to provide adequate mechanisms to bring political crisis to an end. We analyse why international human rights as a political form failed to stem these instances of large-scale, organized violence.

Part IV: From Violence to Justice? The Future of Human Rights
This last section brings the course to a conclusion by examining why and how human rights have been used to bring perpetrators of mass violence to justice, to be held accountable for their past actions in the wake of large-scale human rights violation. It will analyse the post-conflict situation in Cambodia, Rwanda and Nepal and address the questions of truth commissions, international justice trials, accountability and political transformations. The last week brings the course to a conclusion by re-analysing the discourses of human rights and the question of relativism in light of the theoretical concepts and case studies the students have analysed during the course.

Course Materials
There is no required textbook for this course. Students with a longstanding interest in human rights may consider purchasing Violence in War and Peace: An Anthology edited by Nancy Scheper-Hughes and Philippe Bourgois (2003) and ethnographies like Prisoners of Freedom: Human Rights and the African Poor by Harri Englund (2006), Michael Taussig (2003) Law in a Lawless Land: Diary of a Limpieza in Colombia and, Philip Gourevitch (1999) We wish to inform you that tomorrow we will be killed with our families: stories from Rwanda. These works will be discussed as we go through the course.

Most required reading materials will be available in the library, on the Internet and Moodle

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Anthropology of Gender, Sexuality, and The Law
courses.description: This course will be a cross-cultural and historical study of the contexts in which gender and sexuality are articulated and contested in law. Premised on a social constructivist understanding of gender and sexuality, the course aims to provide a set of tools for students to understand and analyze the norms and frameworks regulating human sexuality through the law. The course further locates the making of gender and sexuality in the law within histories of colonialism and imperialism. Students will learn to evaluate different legislative and judicial responses to issues directly related to sexuality such as consent, rape and adultery, prostitution and human trafficking, violence against women, homosexuality, same-sex and heterosexual marriage etc. They will also learn to examine how legal regulation of gender and sexuality extends into other areas of the law about urban space, inheritance, citizenship, immigration and asylum, as well as the prison system. The course aims at providing students with the critical tools to analyze the cultural and historical constructions that inform “laws in the books, laws in the mind, and laws in action.”

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Archaeology of China
courses.description: This course will discuss the history and development of Chinese archaeology, the subjects, research methods and theories of archaeology in mainland China, the formation of the Paleolithic and Neolithic cultures in China, and significant archaeological discoveries of the Bronze Age and historical periods. It will examine how archaeology is related to the construction of Chinese identity and nationalism, and related academic debates. It will also re-evaluate ancient Chinese civilization from the perspectives of ancient Asia and the world. Students will read the primary literature and will be expected to write a research paper.
courses.learning_outcomes:
After taking this course, students are expected to:
1) know the natural and cultural contexts of archaeology in China
2) have a basic understanding of the major issues of Chinese archaeology
3) understand ancient cultural developments and human evolution in China, and the influences of these developments upon contemporary Chinese and Asian cultures.
4) know how archaeological work is related to the political and economic issues in contemporary China
5) cultivate the abilities of cross-cultural, inter-disciplinary and critical thinking
courses.course_syllabus:
The development of Chinese archaeology in the past decades has completely reshaped our knowledge about human and cultural developments in a landmass called China today. This course will discuss the history and development of Chinese archaeology, the subjects, theories, and research approaches of archaeology in mainland China, how archaeology is related to the construction of Chinese identity and nationalism, as well as academic problems and debates.

Major contents of this course are as follows:
1) Introduction- the natural context of human and cultural evolution in China
2) The cultural context of Chinese archaeology
3) Important discoveries of Chinese archaeology from the Palaeolithic, the Neolithic to the historical epoch.
4) Who were the ancestors of contemporary “Chinese＂? Debates on the origin of modern human beings in China.
5) “Central＂ vs. “peripheries＂: who created Chinese civilization?
6) Marxism vs. “the others＂: the theoretical framework of Chinese archaeology.
7) Comparative study: how archaeology in China differs from that in the West?
8) Chinese archaeology in a globalized world today: problems and issues.

Learning activities:

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Preserving Cultural Heritage
courses.description: This course aims to give students the basic knowledge and training on cultural heritage preservation, including archaelogical excavation, report and analysis, and the preservation of ancient architectures and monuments. The course includes the following topics: 1) concepts and international conventions/policies of cultural heritage preservation; 2) archaeological excavation: methods, procedures and standards; 3) archaelogical recording and analysing; and 4) preservation of ancient architectures and monuments: standards and procedures. Students are required to participate in fieldwork and to write a research paper based upon course reading and fieldwork.
courses.learning_outcomes:
After taking this course, students are expected to:
1) understand the basic concepts, principles and approaches of managing cultural heritage.
2) learn to appreciate cultural heritage created by human beings, and to respect different cultures.
3) understand the economic, social and political issues of heritage preservation and management in contemporary societies.
4) cultivate the ability of inter-disciplinary thinking and critical thinking.
5) broaden the academic horizons and knowledge.
courses.course_syllabus:
Shall we preserve the old things, and why? What is “cultural heritage”? Using examples in different parts of the world, this course aims to give students a concise and critical understanding on heritage conservation from an anthropological perspective. The course will introduce basic concepts and cultural contexts of the occurrence and development of cultural heritage conservation in the world, and discuss important issues in this field, including the economic, social and political meanings of heritage in contemporary societies, the impetus of preserving heritage, and the use of heritage as a social and political implement by the state, scholars, and different communities for their own interests. The course will also discuss
problems and challenges in this area. No prior knowledge on heritage preservation is required for this course.

Major contents of this course are as follows:
1) Why are human beings interested in their past? Are all heritage “invented”? The origin and development of heritage conservation.
2) Debates on heritage preservation and management:
a. Who need cultural heritage? Is heritage conservation a social elite business?
b. Who own the cultural heritage, and who have the right to decide what should be preserved, and how to preserve?
c. International principles and local cultures, globalization and localization: the preservation of cultural heritage in different political, economic and social contexts/countries- should there be “universal principles and philosophy” on heritage
conservation? Is there a so-called “best practice”? Who has the right to decide what is “the best practice”?
d. The use and abuse of cultural heritage.
3) Heritage and indigenous people’s right.
4) The future of human beings’ past: can heritage be preserved at all?

Course requirements:
Two one-hour lectures and one one-hour tutorial per week, including a group presentation.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Deciphering the Past: Culture, Archaeology and Science
courses.description: How we understand the past defines the way how we understand our current situation. Archaeology is a dynamic discipline that has tremendously expanded our knowledge about the past, but this subject is not just about digging and doing fieldwork. A wide range of new techniques (e.g., metallurgy, zoology, and 3d stimulation) and research methods have been incorporated into current archaeological research, and eventually transformed the understanding of ourselves and our culture in many ways. This course provides a general introduction in terms of two specific domains: 1) basic archaeological science that changed the research paradigm of human culture and history; 2) an overall history about ancient technology illustrated by new research techniques to explain how this modern world took shape. Moreover, this course tries to cultivate students’ cross-disciplinary research skills and prepare them for the arrival of a new, digitalized research era.

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Archaeology of Food
courses.description: Why study past diets? The study of past human diet and nutrition is a key area of research in archaeology and anthropology and holds significant potential for developing a better understanding of human nutrition today. Our eating habits, biologically and culturally, are often rooted in ancient traditions of past millennia but may also reflect recent changes to society and the environment. Through lectures, discussion groups, and practical lab experiences, this course will provide students with advanced knowledge of the main theoretical and methodological approaches to studying nutrition in the ancient past. Major focuses will include stable isotope analyses, zooarchaeology, and archaeobotany.
courses.learning_outcomes:
By the end of this course, students will:

* Gain an appreciation for the deep history of diverse food systems around the world.
* Garner a broad understanding of the major trends and theoretical frameworks related to food-related research in archaeology.
* Demonstrate a firm understanding of basic isotopic, zooarchaeological, and paleoethnobotanical techniques and how they can be used to analyse and interpret archaeological data.
* Critique isotopic, faunal, and botanical data presented in archaeological literature

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Making Places: Landscapes, Culture and Society
courses.description:
Landscape is a reflection of past interactions between people and their physical environment, which cumulatively create highly recognizable and culturally distinctive places. Such unique and geographically-defined records of particular groups and their way of life are what UNESCO calls “cultural landscapes” (Rössler 2006). Landscapes also reflect and embody intangible beliefs and if we are to understand such ‘non-material’ meanings we must embrace both Western and non-Western (e.g. Chinese) approaches to their study. Hong Kong’s cultural landscape is overwhelmingly urban and modern in character, embedded within, beyond and beneath the city lie other ‘hidden’ landscapes reflecting more ancient belief systems and traditional practices such as agrarian and maritime lifeways and their ‘traditional’ belief systems. Also, Hong Kong has many culturally important ‘ephemeral’ landscapes, relating to the temporary transformation of spaces, for example during religious festivals, or even the more routine transformations that occur at street eateries (dai pai dong) or markets.

This course explores the concept “landscape”, its tangible and intangible dimensions, how they are physically evidenced locally and abroad, and how anthropologists, archaeologists and a myriad of other disciplines approach their study and interpretation. In particular, we will work through a series of local case studies to see what landscape can tell us about the lifeways, economies, politics and beliefs of past and present communities in Hong Kong. By studying cultural landscapes we can also identify what past and present communities, organisations and governments chose to keep and protect and what they let go – by assessing such processes we can develop an understanding of the underlying socio-political and economic drivers at work through time. In terms of heritage management, therefore, if we wish to militate against the gradual loss of meaning and value in our cultural landscapes, a landscape approach is indicated.
courses.course_syllabus:
Major Topics

• Concept, history, use and understanding of “landscape” in Western and non-Western contexts

• Landscape as a bridge between disciplines and facilitator of new dialogues

• Anthropologies and Archaeologies of Landscape

• Legislation and Guidelines for Landscape: from World Heritage to Local Interpretations

• Contested Spaces: Landscapes as Arenas for Conflict, Resistance and Negotiation

• Historic Urban Landscape: Hong Kong, Guangzhou and Macau

• Before the Metropolis: Social Landscapes and Sustainability in Pre-urban Hong Kong

• Exploring the Intangible: Hong Kong’s Ephemeral Landscapes

• Review: Assessing the Causes, Effects and Future Implications of Hong Kong’s ‘Landscape-less’ Approach to Heritage Management

Two 45 minute lectures and one 45 minute tutorial per week for one semester, plus a field trip to explore a cultural landscape in Hong Kong.

courses.title: Archaeological Field Study
courses.description:
This course will enable students to extend their archaeological learning in the classroom to an archaeological field site. The course combines a set of standard in-class lectures and tutorials with an 8-12 day field study trip to a location typically outside Hong Kong. The field study trip will consist of both supervised student-led field research and formal face-to-face teaching including such things as guest lectures with local experts, formal professor-guided class discussions on methodology and archaeological fieldwork, guided museum tours, and local study tours focused on the cultural, political, and economic lives of local people. Students will form small groups to investigate different archaeological topics within the field site.

Open only to anthropology majors.
The contents of this course will vary with different instructors and students. Offerings under the same course code, but with different field sites can be taken for credit, up to a maximum of two times.
courses.learning_outcomes:
Upon completion of this course students will:

1) have developed practical archaeological fieldwork skills in a real-world environment
2) be able to understand more fully the complexities of archaeological fieldwork
3) be able to understand more fully how to collect real-world archaeological data, analyse these, and properly present and write them up
4) have a deeper understanding of cultural and historical differences an in-depth experience with a particular historical culture.
courses.course_syllabus:
Field sites and topics will vary depending on the Professor offering and accompanying students on the field trip. See Syllabus below.

Because each field study will significantly differ in its particulars, it is impossible to offer a full syllabus. However, each course offered will follow the broad principles listed below:

Archaeological Field Study will have

1) Pre-field study preparation involving three – eight weeks (depending on whether the course is to be offered during the Fall / Spring term or during the Summer Session) of lectures, tutorials, and reading requirements. The field study itself, involving 8-12 days of archaeological or archaeological- related fieldwork (such as museum-based field research), will be closely overseen by the course instructor and will include up to three hours per day
of formal classroom instruction which will add up to no less than 12 hours for the trip as a whole.
2) A group report, a final paper, and some form of knowledge-transfer.

A tentative weekly schedule is as follows: Week 1: Introduction
Week 2: Principles of Archaeological Fieldwork
Week 3: Archaeological Artifacts Analysis and Lab Work
Week 4 – 8: Site-specific topics (Students will begin to explore archaeological methods in use at the site as well as their own sets of questions for group investigation)
Week 9–10: Will be held in the field site (12 hours of formal contact over the course of the 8-12 days of the field trip) Week 11-13: Presentations and Final Case Analysis

A tentative 8 - 12 day schedule at the field site:
Day 1: Arrival and introduction; meetings with local students and instructor(s) at destination (Destination: to be decided) Day 2: Site visits; group interviews; site orientation and research topic discussions
Day 3: Visit to local cultural sites; group interviews; participant observation with specialists on selected research topics
Day 4: Archaeological artifacts analysis and lab visit; Site visits and work; group interviews; archaeological/museum work on selected research topics Day 5: Guest lectures and workshops; site visits and work; archaeological/museum work on selected research topics
Day 6: Archaeological artifacts analysis and lab visit; Site visits and work; archaeological/museum work on selected research topics Day 7: Visit to local cultural sites; group interviews; participant observation with specialists on selected research topics
Day 8: Archaeological artifacts analysis and lab visit; Site visits and work; group interviews; archaeological/museum work on selected research topics Day 9: Guest lectures and workshops; site visits and work; archaeological/museum work on selected research topics
Day 10: Archaeological artifacts analysis and lab visit; Site visits and work; group interviews; archaeological/museum work on selected research topics
Day 11: Group presentations, larger course-level group analyses and discussions, and wrap up Day 12: Departure and return to Hong Kong

courses.subject: ANTH
courses.title: Human Evolution
courses.description: What does it mean to be human? Where did we come from? Where are we going? This courses investigates long-term evolutionary perspectives on the human species. The basics of evolution and natural selection as scientific theories are clearly set out and examined, and common misconceptions discussed. Evidence for the evolution of mammals and primates is reviewed and discussed, and the common characteristics of these species are highlighted, demonstrating the connections between humans and other forms of life. The course covers what we know about human ancestors and the evolution of modern humans. Students are introduced to the wide range of human adaptations to local conditions across contemporary cultures and the variety of relationships that human populations have with the environment. Students are encouraged to use the knowledge they have acquired to ask; are these relationships always sustainable? Looking to the future; what are our responsibilities both to future generations of humans and towards other species with which we share our world? This course aims to give students an understanding and appreciation of evolutionary perspectives on the place of humans in the world, the variety of contemporary human societies, and a broad perspective on the complexity of the relationship between humans, the environment and other species.
courses.learning_outcomes:
In this course students learn about the nature of scientific theories and their development, as well as the use of evidence in evaluating hypotheses. Students are also exposed to the potential for misunderstandings of scientific theory and the distinction between fact and value. Comparative abilities are emphasized through reviewing common features of the life-course of a variety of animals and the influence of animal habitats, with particular focus on closely related primate species.

The history of human evolution is introduced to students, focusing on the emergence of universal capacities such as language, technology, art and culture. Students are encouraged to learn about and appreciate the variety of human cultures and the flexibility of humans in adapting to local environments. A comparative perspective on human culture is encouraged through a focus on the common subsistence needs of all humans, and the variety of practices by which these needs are met.

Students are exposed to a wide perspective on the place of the human species in the world. They are encouraged to exercise long-term evaluations of, and exercise a sense of judgement about the impact and sustainability of human action, both in relation to the environment and other species as well as future generations of the human species. Students are thus encouraged to think about their own place in society.
courses.course_syllabus:
This course investigates long-term evolutionary perspectives on the human species. We will discover those human characteristics that connect us to and make us different from other species and come to better understand ourselves and our place in the world.

We discuss the variety of relationships that human populations today have with other species and the natural environment. The course encourages us to ask: are these relationships always sustainable? Looking to the future; what are our responsibilities both to future generations of humans and towards other species with which we share our world?

Latest course information available on WebCT or Moodle.

Course Structure:
Each week will introduce a topic or set of concepts that will be covered by the lectures and by about 20-30 pages of key readings. The lectures will structure each topic in a simple way, providing explanations and examples so that the basic ideas are understood. Students will benefit by taking brief notes during the lectures.
Questions are very welcome, both during the lectures and especially during the later tutorial.
All of the reading material will be readily available either in the U Li. reserve collection or online/on the webCT site. Each week, students are expected to read, think about, and mentally summarise the readings before the tutorial.
The tutorial provides an opportunity for students to discuss the readings, raise questions and debate the ideas, and consolidate their understanding. Normally, tutorials will open with a short (less than 5 minutes) informal summary of the readings covered that week, given by a student. All other tutorial members will be expected to contribute to the discussion. The aims of the tutorials are
• to enable students to make summaries of the readings and topics of their choice;
• to raise and discuss questions, experience and perspectives about the concepts and the reading material;
• to enable students to make suggestions for the improvement of the course/ lectures/ readings etc.
